n: The day of the Lord is coming. Jerusalem will be plundered, and the loot divided right in its streets.

God will allow all nations to attack Jerusalem. The city will be captured and suffer terribly; half will go into exile, but a remnant will stay. Latter-day Saints associate this with the battle of Armageddon before Christ’s coming.

f.w: I will gather all nations against Jerusalem

n: Then the Lord Himself will go out and fight those nations, as He fought for Israel in the past.

f.w: as when he fought in the day of battle

n: His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and it will split in two, creating a great valley. Modern revelation confirms this will happen at the Savior’s Second Coming. Jesus ascended from this mountain, and angels promised He would return the same way.

f.w: his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives

n: People will flee through the new valley as they fled the earthquake in King Uzziah’s day. Then the Lord will come with all His holy ones.

f.w: the earthquake in the days of Uzziah

f.g: An unknown place, perhaps near Jerusalem.

n: On that day the light will be strange — neither clear nor dark.

f.w: the light shall not be clear
f.g: Perhaps “there will be no cold or frost” — the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: It will be a unique day known only to the Lord, neither day nor night — and at evening there will be light. Hope dawns when it seems darkest.

f.w: which shall be known to the LORD
at evening time it shall be light

n: Living water will flow from Jerusalem, half to the Dead Sea and half to the Mediterranean, year-round. Ezekiel and Joel saw the same healing river.

f.w: living waters shall go out from Jerusalem

f.g: The eastern sea — the Dead Sea.

n: The Lord will be King over all the earth — one Lord, with one name. This is the Millennium, when Christ reigns personally.

f.w: the LORD shall be king over all the earth
one LORD, and his name one

n: The land around Jerusalem will become a plain, while Jerusalem is lifted high and fully inhabited, from gate to gate.

f.g: From the northern to the southern edge of Judah.

n: People will live there safely; never again will it be devoted to destruction.

f.g: No more curse or ban (Hebrew ḥerem).

n: A terrible plague will strike those who fought Jerusalem: their flesh, eyes, and tongues will rot while they stand.
The Lord will send panic among the enemies, so they turn on each other.

f.w: his hand shall rise up against the hand of his neighbour

n: Judah will also fight at Jerusalem, and the wealth of the nations — gold, silver, clothing — will be collected in abundance.

f.w: the wealth of all the heathen

n: The same plague will strike the enemy’s horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all their animals.

f.g: The same plague described in verse 12.

n: Survivors from the hostile nations will go to Jerusalem every year to worship the King and celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles. Former enemies become worshipers.
Any nation that refuses to come worship the King will receive no rain.

f.w: upon them shall be no rain

n: Even Egypt, which depended on the Nile rather than rain, will be struck with plague if it refuses.

f.g: Egypt relied on the Nile, not rainfall, so it receives a plague instead.

n: This will be the punishment for Egypt and every nation that won’t come to keep the feast.

f.g: Literally “the sin” — the consequence of the sin.

n: In that day even horses’ bells will be engraved “Holiness unto the Lord” — the words once on the high priest’s headpiece. Ordinary cooking pots will be as sacred as altar bowls. Everything will be holy. Latter-day Saints see these words inscribed on temples today.

f.g: Sacred basins used in temple sacrifices.

n: Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy, usable for sacred meals, and no trader will be found in the Lord’s house. Jesus cleansed the temple of merchants, foreshadowing this.

f.w: no more the Canaanite in the house of the LORD
